comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'After talking to Patrick about this in more detail, we think there’s an ordering issue between when we upgrade the OSDs and when we set values for the preferred ciphers and service cipher. I'd agree with Adam that we haven't had enough runtime with BlueStore and 16K.", 'marks': [{'type': 'em'}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': '7c90545c5ad2'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "I think longer term we probably do want min_alloc_size = 16K but with deferred_write_size = 0 (which I think means the device block size?). With the logical capacity being 6x physical capacity we can afford the min_alloc_size being larger and will benefit from the allocator using less memory and getting less fragmented at the expense of using slightly more of the logical capacity (in a pathological scenario where you fill a FCM with random 4K writes we will be limited to 1.5:1 compression because we are using 4x the logical capacity for every write, real world scenarios will have many writes >4K and won't achieve much better than 2:1 compression so we'll run out of physical capacity first).", 'marks': [{'type': 'em'}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': '974d219ea549'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The only performance results which will noticeably change will be for <16K I/Os. Assuming BlueStore is only using min_alloc_size for space allocation and is using the device block size for aligning I/O requests (I think this is the case) then it will only be <16K write I/Os that are affected. My guess is that this will improve performance for <16K writes by avoiding the FCM from having to do a read-modify-write to merge the new data into an existing 16K block. Making discards work properly for this workload will also improve performance when the FCM is nearly full.', 'marks': [{'type': 'em'}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'cc84d235ae93'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "I think we need a plan for getting more coverage in BlueStore with a min_alloc_size of 16K, this doesn't all have to be on systems with FCMs - we are mainly looking for issues/unexpected behavior in BlueStore. We would need to do this testing downstream, initially by getting testers to manually increase min_alloc_size as they deploy clusters.", 'marks': [{'type': 'em'}]}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'We will use the original documentation ticket to remove the 16K min_alloc_size config override in 9.1 documentation '}, {'type': 'inlineCard', 'attrs': {'url': 'https://ibm-ceph.atlassian.net/browse/ISCE-3978', 'localId': 'bfc5dac21c80'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' and use this bug to fix the code in a future release. Removing the blocker flag from this ticket and changing target release.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '959ee8bd1d15'}}]}

description:
{'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Description of problem - '}], 'attrs': {'localId': '108489ffcd7f'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': 'e9d0adf9ec79'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "recent recommendations from RedHat to deploy 2 to 4 OSDs per NVME drive for deployments that support many small objects, and dense servers that have many drives, we've reached the stage where the default Ceph configurations aren't enough.

Our servers have 48 drives, and we deploy 2 OSDs per drive - reaching 96 OSDs.

This is similar to the following KB: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7092293?band=se&seSessionId=800334f7-f18e-4a2d-bcd1-78eda4fd5080&seSource=Recommendation&seResourceOriginID=fbf02fa0-6ea0-4452-b9c8-7e10ce93322d

But since we are colocating MGRs and MONs with our OSDs, the current range is not enough.

We would like for the Ceph service in firewall-cmd to be increased further, and for the ms_bind_port_max default configuration to be increased as well."}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Version-Release number of selected component (if applicable):'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '88f6810bdc19'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '8.1.z3'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '6a5ecb93a64b'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Does this issue impact your ability to continue to work with the product?'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'a6027b1480b6'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'It impacts communication protocols of the osds beyond the ports available.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '0add3a1b24b8'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Is there any workaround available to the best of your knowledge?'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'd4b6eedc14a5'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': '633d61341eb8'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '[global]

With this approach, “state” would mean: “the server did not receive host for TTL”, not “host reported an old clock value” and it would work even with clock skew during bootstrap. Also, I think it would better fit our reconcile loop philosophy: use what provisioner really observes.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '91fd86572ef4'}}]}

When we list daemons, the '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'VersionStatusUpdater', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' class is responsible for determining the version of each daemon. It already has dedicated handling for several daemon types such as NFS, iSCSI, Prometheus, Grafana, etc.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'c131ea180d3c'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "What I noticed is that the agent daemon type isn't included in that logic. The agent is a little different from the other daemons because it runs as a native Python process rather than inside a container. As a result, the existing version detection mechanism doesn't work for it since there's no container to exec into and query the version."}], 'attrs': {'localId': '21100c63a65e'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "So at the moment, it looks like the version information for the agent daemon simply isn't being collected, which explains why it ends up showing as "}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '<unknown>', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ". We'll need to handle the agent differently and implement a separate way to retrieve and report its version information."}], 'attrs': {'localId': '8490cdcdb60f'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'CC: '}, {'type': 'mention', 'attrs': {'id': '712020:0602f1f0-07ff-43ab-b637-833f1b99dd32', 'text': '@Prashant Dhange', 'accessLevel': '', 'localId': 'f7800315-6a3e-4091-b4ce-e8d57215d844'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' '}], 'attrs': {'localId': '05fc83a153eb'}}]}

We weren't able to add them because of the problem in this...
description:
{'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Description of problem - '}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "Our cluster started having lc problems one week ago, and the lc in the cluster hasn't been able to finish. We have four servers, and on each server two gateways. 
This problem happened two months ago and we tried to add two more RGW per server. We weren't able to add them because of the problem in this case 04422449.
The lc worker RGW_LC_MAX_WP_WORKER and RGW_LC_MAX_WORKER are set at seven, any suggestions on what we can do?"}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Version-Release number of selected component (if applicable): 8.1.z6'}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "There's also a known issue in RHCS 8.1z6 for RGW segfaulting in `RGWIndexCompletionManager::create_completion()` during object delete operations in lifecycle cleanup [1][2].  This is currently targeted to be fixed in RHCS 8.1z7.

[1] https://ibm-ceph.atlassian.net/browse/IBMCEPH-12966
[2] https://ibm-ceph.atlassian.net/browse/IBMCEPH-14805"}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Current situation we are unable regardless of parameters,  or restarting RGW to get the processes to finish.  '}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The ask here is as of sunday this was the situation:'}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'We have 234 LC operations in PROCESSING
184 from yesterday
38 from today
12 from two days ago.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'users delete millions of objects on a daily basis and the retention policy is a day.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'rgw lc threads have been segragated. '}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'They are running 7 threads per instance'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'normally the schedule is between 3am an 9am ( I’ll verify that. )'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'In order to stop the lc processes we changed enabled_threads =false '}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'and restarted the rgw instances. '}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'after which ran manually:'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'radosgw-admin lc process --bucket=<name>   the policy peaked for a few moments but hasn’t progressed.'}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'There was a peak in 03:00-03:05 with 10k op/s, but then the operations were about 80~ op/s.
The lc_max_worker is currently 5.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The ask is: how do we force the lc policies to run?  '}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'I have also suggested that the change this to a 24x7 run   changing the schedule to 00:01 - 23:59.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Logs collected and log location: supportshell_eu case  04465650'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Additional info:'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'We simply looking for additional guidance to help mitigate this  since adding threads seems to cause additional latency.'}]}]}

curl -u "admin:superuser" -s -k -X GET https://9.11.121.74/redfish/v1/Systems/Self/EthernetInterfaces | jq . { \xa0 "@odata.context": "/redfish/v1/$metadata#EthernetInterfaceCollection.EthernetInterfaceCollection", \xa0 "@odata.etag": "\"1770714069\"", \xa0 "@odata.id": "/redfish/v1/Systems/Self/EthernetInterfaces", \xa0 "@odata.type": "#EthernetInterfaceCollection.EthernetInterfaceCollection", \xa0 "Description": "Collection of ethernet interfaces for this system", \xa0 "Members": [], \xa0 "Members@odata.count": 0, \xa0 "Name": "Ethernet Interface Collection" } #'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '\xa0'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The same request sent to different hosts gives different results.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '\xa0'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Also, some other examples of instability observed:'}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'language': 'code-java'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '# curl -v -o- -D- -u "admin:superuser" -s -k -X GET https://9.11.121.74/redfish/v1/Systems * \xa0 Trying 9.11.121.74:443... * connect to 9.11.121.74 port 443 failed: Connection refused * Failed to connect to 9.11.121.74 port 443: Connection refused * Closing connection 0 # curl -o- -D- -u "admin:superuser" -s -k -X GET https://9.11.121.74/redfish/v1/Systems HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: AMI MegaRAC Redfish Service Allow: GET'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The first request fails with "connection refused", and the very next identical request immediately succeeds with an HTTP 200.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '\xa0'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "There's no indication on the cause but some endpoints may fail like the following:"}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '\xa0'}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'language': 'code-java'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '2026-02-16 09:40:08,626 - ceph_node_proxy.redfish_client - WARNING - HTTP query error: 500 Internal Server Error — 
[web.lua] Error in RequestHandler, thread: 0x75a301a8 is dead.
2026-02-16 09:40:08,626 - ceph_node_proxy.redfish:Endpoint - ERROR - HTTP error while querying /redfish/v1/Systems/Self/EthernetInterfaces/EthernetInterface1 - 500 - Internal Server Error \xa0 '}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'On one of the server (9.11.121.47), the Redfish API is no longer working at all, each query results in a 503 error (which makes the agent restarting in a loop):'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '\xa0'}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'language': 'code-java'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "[16/Feb/2026:09:18:36] ENGINE Bus STARTED 2026-02-16 09:18:36,390 - ceph_node_proxy.api - INFO - node-proxy API started. 2026-02-16 09:18:37,011 - ceph_node_proxy.redfish_client - WARNING - Got 503 from /redfish/v1/, reason: Service Not Available 2026-02-16 09:18:37,011 - ceph_node_proxy.redfish_client - ERROR - Can't discover SessionService url: HTTP Error 503: Service Not Available"}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '\xa0'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'These behaviors suggest instability in the redfish API.'}]}]}

atollon(8)                                                                           Atollon Management Utilities                                                                          atollon(8)

NAME
       atollon - Atollon management CLI

SYNOPSIS
       atollon [sub-command] [option...]

DESCRIPTION
       The atollon command provides a set of sub-commands to help manage Ceph on Atollon hardware. The following components and features are supported

           - Node firmware
           - FCM firmware
           - Drive slot management
           - Device listing
           - Node metadata
           - Chassis identification

       Firmware related sub-commands can be long-running, so use of a terminal multiplexer like tmux or screen is recommended.

ATOLLON SUB-COMMANDS
       chassis
           Turn the chassis/enclosure IDENT LED on or off, or check it's current state
       device
           List the devices in slot sequence assigned to the node
       fcm-update
           Update the firmware of a specific FCM device
       node-info
           Show metadata describing the node inclduing OS, platform and device firmware levels
       node-upgrade
           Upgrade the platform firmware (BMC, BIOS, FPGA etc)
       slot
           Manage a specific Atollon device slot

EXAMPLES
       Show device information:
       atollon device -l

       Perform a concurrent firmware update of an FCM device:
       atollon fcm-update -i makemake_cust-A5.3.6.73.bin -d nvme2n1 --with-reset

       Power a drive slot off:
       atollon slot --id 1 --power off --force

       Turn on the chassis IDENT LED for the current node:
       atollon chassis --ident on

BUGS
       1. FCM device that experience errors at discover may result in device listing errors, since slot enumeration
          fails. If this occurs, use a different sort sequence to show the devices

AUTHOR
       Written and maintained by Paul Cuzner <pcuzner@ibm.com>.

REPORTING BUGS
       Patches and issues may be submitted to the IBM github repo at <https://github.ibm.com/ceph/atollon-utils>.

SEE ALSO
       atollon-chassis(8), atollon-device(8), atollon-fcm-update(8), atollon-fcm-bulk-update(8), atollon-node-info(8), atollon-node-update(8), atollon-slot(8)

Exporter(3)                                                                      User Contributed Perl Documentation                                                                      Exporter(3)

NAME
       Exporter - Implements default import method for modules

SYNOPSIS
       In module YourModule.pm:

         package YourModule;
         use Exporter 'import';
         our @EXPORT_OK = qw(munge frobnicate);  # symbols to export on request

       or

         package YourModule;
         require Exporter;
         our @ISA = qw(Exporter);  # inherit all of Exporter's methods
         our @EXPORT_OK = qw(munge frobnicate);  # symbols to export on request

       or

         package YourModule;
         use parent 'Exporter';  # inherit all of Exporter's methods
         our @EXPORT_OK = qw(munge frobnicate);  # symbols to export on request

       In other files which wish to use "YourModule":

         use YourModule qw(frobnicate);      # import listed symbols
         frobnicate ($left, $right)          # calls YourModule::frobnicate

       Take a look at "Good Practices" for some variants you will like to use in modern Perl code.

DESCRIPTION
       The Exporter module implements an "import" method which allows a module to export functions and variables to its users' namespaces.  Many modules use Exporter rather than implementing their
       own "import" method because Exporter provides a highly flexible interface, with an implementation optimised for the common case.

       Perl automatically calls the "import" method when processing a "use" statement for a module.  Modules and "use" are documented in perlfunc and perlmod.  Understanding the concept of modules
       and how the "use" statement operates is important to understanding the Exporter.

   How to Export
       The arrays @EXPORT and @EXPORT_OK in a module hold lists of symbols that are going to be exported into the users name space by default, or which they can request to be exported,
       respectively.  The symbols can represent functions, scalars, arrays, hashes, or typeglobs.  The symbols must be given by full name with the exception that the ampersand in front of a
       function is optional, e.g.

         our @EXPORT    = qw(afunc $scalar @array);   # afunc is a function
         our @EXPORT_OK = qw(&bfunc %hash *typeglob); # explicit prefix on &bfunc

       If you are only exporting function names it is recommended to omit the ampersand, as the implementation is faster this way.

   Selecting What to Export
       Do not export method names!

       Do not export anything else by default without a good reason!

       Exports pollute the namespace of the module user.  If you must export try to use @EXPORT_OK in preference to @EXPORT and avoid short or common symbol names to reduce the risk of name
       clashes.

       Generally anything not exported is still accessible from outside the module using the "YourModule::item_name" (or "$blessed_ref->method") syntax.  By convention you can use a leading
       underscore on names to informally indicate that they are 'internal' and not for public use.

       (It is actually possible to get private functions by saying:
 my $subref = sub { ... };
         $subref->(@args);            # Call it as a function
         $obj->$subref(@args);        # Use it as a method

       However if you use them for methods it is up to you to figure out how to make inheritance work.)

       As a general rule, if the module is trying to be object oriented then export nothing.  If it's just a collection of functions then @EXPORT_OK anything but use @EXPORT with caution.  For
       function and method names use barewords in preference to names prefixed with ampersands for the export lists.

       Other module design guidelines can be found in perlmod.

   How to Import
       In other files which wish to use your module there are three basic ways for them to load your module and import its symbols:

       "use YourModule;"
           This imports all the symbols from YourModule's @EXPORT into the namespace of the "use" statement.

       "use YourModule ();"
           This causes perl to load your module but does not import any symbols.

       "use YourModule qw(...);"
           This imports only the symbols listed by the caller into their namespace.  All listed symbols must be in your @EXPORT or @EXPORT_OK, else an error occurs.  The advanced export features of
           Exporter are accessed like this, but with list entries that are syntactically distinct from symbol names.

       Unless you want to use its advanced features, this is probably all you need to know to use Exporter.

Advanced Features
   Specialised Import Lists
       If any of the entries in an import list begins with !, : or / then the list is treated as a series of specifications which either add to or delete from the list of names to import.  They are
       processed left to right. Specifications are in the form:

           [!]name         This name only
           [!]:DEFAULT     All names in @EXPORT
           [!]:tag         All names in $EXPORT_TAGS{tag} anonymous array
           [!]/pattern/    All names in @EXPORT and @EXPORT_OK which match

       A  leading ! indicates that matching names should be deleted from the list of names to import.  If the first specification is a deletion it is treated as though preceded by :DEFAULT.  If you
       just want to import extra names in addition to the default set you will still need to include :DEFAULT explicitly.

       e.g., Module.pm defines:

           our @EXPORT      = qw(A1 A2 A3 A4 A5);
           our @EXPORT_OK   = qw(B1 B2 B3 B4 B5);
           our %EXPORT_TAGS = (T1 => [qw(A1 A2 B1 B2)], T2 => [qw(A1 A2 B3 B4)]);

       Note that you cannot use tags in @EXPORT or @EXPORT_OK.

       Names in EXPORT_TAGS must also appear in @EXPORT or @EXPORT_OK.

       An application using Module can say something like:

           use Module qw(:DEFAULT :T2 !B3 A3);

       Other examples include:

           use Socket qw(!/^[AP]F_/ !SOMAXCONN !SOL_SOCKET);
           use POSIX  qw(:errno_h :termios_h !TCSADRAIN !/^EXIT/);

       Remember that most patterns (using //) will need to be anchored with a leading ^, e.g., "/^EXIT/" rather than "/EXIT/".

       You can say "BEGIN { $Exporter::Verbose=1 }" to see how the specifications are being processed and what is actually being imported into modules.

 Exporting Without Using Exporter's import Method
       Exporter has a special method, 'export_to_level' which is used in situations where you can't directly call Exporter's import method.  The export_to_level method looks like:

           MyPackage->export_to_level(
               $where_to_export, $package, @what_to_export
           );

       where $where_to_export is an integer telling how far up the calling stack to export your symbols, and @what_to_export is an array telling what symbols *to* export (usually this is @_).   The
       $package argument is currently unused.

       For example, suppose that you have a module, A, which already has an import function:

           package A;

           our @ISA = qw(Exporter);
           our @EXPORT_OK = qw($b);

           sub import
           {
               $A::b = 1;     # not a very useful import method
           }

       and you want to Export symbol $A::b back to the module that called package A.  Since Exporter relies on the import method to work, via inheritance, as it stands Exporter::import() will never
       get called.  Instead, say the following:

           package A;
           our @ISA = qw(Exporter);
           our @EXPORT_OK = qw($b);

           sub import
           {
               $A::b = 1;
               A->export_to_level(1, @_);
           }

       This will export the symbols one level 'above' the current package - ie: to the program or module that used package A.

       Note: Be careful not to modify @_ at all before you call export_to_level - or people using your package will get very unexplained results!

   Exporting Without Inheriting from Exporter
       By  including  Exporter  in your @ISA you inherit an Exporter's import() method but you also inherit several other helper methods which you probably don't want and complicate the inheritance
       tree.  To avoid this you can do:

         package YourModule;
         use Exporter qw(import);

       which will export Exporter's own import() method into YourModule.  Everything will work as before but you won't need to include Exporter in @YourModule::ISA.

       Note: This feature was introduced in version 5.57 of Exporter, released with perl 5.8.3.

Module Version Checking
       The Exporter module will convert an attempt to import a number from a module into a call to "$module_name->VERSION($value)".  This can be used to validate that  the  version  of  the  module
       being used is greater than or equal to the required version.

       For  historical  reasons,  Exporter  supplies  a  "require_version"  method  that  simply  delegates  to  "VERSION".   Originally,  before  "UNIVERSAL::VERSION"  existed, Exporter would call
       "require_version".

       Since the "UNIVERSAL::VERSION" method treats the $VERSION number as a simple numeric value it will regard version 1.10 as lower than 1.9.  For this reason it is strongly recommended that you
       use numbers with at least two decimal places, e.g., 1.09.

   Managing Unknown Symbols
       In some situations you may want to prevent certain symbols from being exported.  Typically this applies to extensions which have functions or constants that may not exist on some systems.

       The names of any symbols that cannot be exported should be listed in the @EXPORT_FAIL array.

       If a module attempts to import any of these symbols the Exporter will give the module an opportunity to handle  the  situation  before  generating  an  error.   The  Exporter  will  call  an
       export_fail method with a list of the failed symbols:

         @failed_symbols = $module_name->export_fail(@failed_symbols);

       If the "export_fail" method returns an empty list then no error is recorded and all the requested symbols are exported.  If the returned list is not empty then an error is generated for each
       symbol and the export fails.  The Exporter provides a default "export_fail" method which simply returns the list unchanged.

       Uses  for the "export_fail" method include giving better error messages for some symbols and performing lazy architectural checks (put more symbols into @EXPORT_FAIL by default and then take
       them out if someone actually tries to use them and an expensive check shows that they are usable on that platform).

   Tag Handling Utility Functions
       Since the symbols listed within %EXPORT_TAGS must also appear in either @EXPORT or @EXPORT_OK, two utility functions are provided which allow you to easily add  tagged  sets  of  symbols  to
       @EXPORT or @EXPORT_OK:

         our %EXPORT_TAGS = (foo => [qw(aa bb cc)], bar => [qw(aa cc dd)]);

         Exporter::export_tags('foo');     # add aa, bb and cc to @EXPORT
         Exporter::export_ok_tags('bar');  # add aa, cc and dd to @EXPORT_OK

       Any  names  which are not tags are added to @EXPORT or @EXPORT_OK unchanged but will trigger a warning (with "-w") to avoid misspelt tags names being silently added to @EXPORT or @EXPORT_OK.
       Future versions may make this a fatal error.

   Generating Combined Tags
       If several symbol categories exist in %EXPORT_TAGS, it's usually useful to create the utility ":all" to simplify "use" statements.

       The simplest way to do this is:

        our  %EXPORT_TAGS = (foo => [qw(aa bb cc)], bar => [qw(aa cc dd)]);

         # add all the other ":class" tags to the ":all" class,
         # deleting duplicates
         {
           my %seen;

           push @{$EXPORT_TAGS{all}},
             grep {!$seen{$_}++} @{$EXPORT_TAGS{$_}} foreach keys %EXPORT_TAGS;
              CGI.pm creates an ":all" tag which contains some (but not really all) of its categories.  That could be done with one small change:

         # add some of the other ":class" tags to the ":all" class,
         # deleting duplicates
         {
           my %seen;

           push @{$EXPORT_TAGS{all}},
             grep {!$seen{$_}++} @{$EXPORT_TAGS{$_}}
               foreach qw/html2 html3 netscape form cgi internal/;
         }

       Note that the tag names in %EXPORT_TAGS don't have the leading ':'.

   "AUTOLOAD"ed Constants
       Many modules make use of "AUTOLOAD"ing for constant subroutines to avoid having to compile and waste memory on rarely used values (see perlsub for details on constant subroutines).  Calls to
       such constant subroutines are not optimized away at compile time because they can't be checked at compile time for constancy.

       Even if a prototype is available at compile time, the body of the subroutine is not (it hasn't been "AUTOLOAD"ed yet).  perl needs to examine both the  "()"  prototype  and  the  body  of  a
       subroutine at compile time to detect that it can safely replace calls to that subroutine with the constant value.

       A workaround for this is to call the constants once in a "BEGIN" block:

          package My ;

          use Socket ;

          foo( SO_LINGER );  ## SO_LINGER NOT optimized away; called at runtime
          BEGIN { SO_LINGER }
          foo( SO_LINGER );  ## SO_LINGER optimized away at compile time.

       This forces the "AUTOLOAD" for "SO_LINGER" to take place before SO_LINGER is encountered later in "My" package.

       If you are writing a package that "AUTOLOAD"s, consider forcing an "AUTOLOAD" for any constants explicitly imported by other packages or which are usually used when your package is "use"d.

Good Practices
   Declaring @EXPORT_OK and Friends
       When using "Exporter" with the standard "strict" and "warnings" pragmas, the "our" keyword is needed to declare the package variables @EXPORT_OK, @EXPORT, @ISA, etc.

         our @ISA = qw(Exporter);
         our @EXPORT_OK = qw(munge frobnicate);

       If backward compatibility for Perls under 5.6 is important, one must write instead a "use vars" statement.

         use vars qw(@ISA @EXPORT_OK);
         @ISA = qw(Exporter);
         @EXPORT_OK = qw(munge frobnicate);

   Playing Safe
       There  are  some  caveats  with  the use of runtime statements like "require Exporter" and the assignment to package variables, which can be very subtle for the unaware programmer.  This may
       happen for instance with mutually recursive modules, which are affected by the time the relevant constructions are executed.

       The ideal way to never have to think about that is to use "BEGIN" blocks and the simple import method.  So the first part of the "SYNOPSIS" code could be rewritten as:

         package YourModule;


 use strict;
         use warnings;

         use Exporter 'import';
         BEGIN {
           our @EXPORT_OK = qw(munge frobnicate);  # symbols to export on request
         }

       Or if you need to inherit from Exporter:

         package YourModule;

         use strict;
         use warnings;

         BEGIN {
           require Exporter;
           our @ISA = qw(Exporter);  # inherit all of Exporter's methods
           our @EXPORT_OK = qw(munge frobnicate);  # symbols to export on request
         }

       The "BEGIN" will assure that the loading of Exporter.pm and the assignments to @ISA and @EXPORT_OK happen immediately like "use", leaving no room for something to  get  awry  or  just  plain
       wrong.

       With respect to loading "Exporter" and inheriting, there are alternatives with the use of modules like "base" and "parent".

         use base qw(Exporter);
         # or
         use parent qw(Exporter);

       Any  of  these  statements  are  nice  replacements  for  "BEGIN  { require Exporter; our @ISA = qw(Exporter); }" with the same compile-time effect.  The basic difference is that "base" code
       interacts with declared "fields" while "parent" is a streamlined version of the older "base" code to just establish the IS-A relationship.

       For more details, see the documentation and code of base and parent.

       Another thorough remedy to that runtime vs. compile-time trap is to use Exporter::Easy, which is a wrapper of Exporter that allows all boilerplate code at a single gulp in the use statement.

          use Exporter::Easy (
              OK => [ qw(munge frobnicate) ],
          );
          # @ISA setup is automatic
          # all assignments happen at compile time

   What Not to Export
       You have been warned already in "Selecting What to Export" to not export:

       •   method names (because you don't need to and that's likely to not do what you want),

       •   anything by default (because you don't want to surprise your users...  badly)

       •   anything you don't need to (because less is more)

       There's one more item to add to this list.  Do not export variable names.  Just because "Exporter" lets you do that, it does not mean you should.

         @EXPORT_OK = qw($svar @avar %hvar); # DON'T!
 Exporting variables is not a good idea.  They can change under the hood, provoking horrible effects at-a-distance that are too hard to track and to fix.  Trust me: they are not worth it.

       To provide the capability to set/get class-wide settings, it is best instead to provide accessors as subroutines or class methods instead.

SEE ALSO
       "Exporter" is definitely not the only module with symbol exporter capabilities.  At CPAN, you may find a bunch of them.  Some are lighter.  Some provide improved APIs and features.  Pick the
       one that fits your needs.  The following is a sample list of such modules.

           Exporter::Easy
           Exporter::Lite
           Exporter::Renaming
           Exporter::Tidy
           Sub::Exporter / Sub::Installer
           Perl6::Export / Perl6::Export::Attrs

NAME
       atollon-exporter - Atollon Prometheus metrics exporter

SYNOPSIS
       atollon exporter [ --port PORT ]

DESCRIPTION
       The  exporter  sub-command starts a basic Prometheus compatible metrics exporter that exposes platform health information over HTTP. The exporter runs as a foreground process and serves met‐
       rics at the /metrics endpoint.

       Metrics provided include hardware health status, drive slot information, platform firmware versions, and temperature and fan sensor readings.

OPTIONS
       --port, -p PORT
           Port to bind the exporter to (default: 10090)

EXAMPLES
       Start the exporter on the default port:
         # atollon exporter

       Start the exporter on a custom port:
         # atollon exporter --port 9100

BUGS
       None reported at this time

AUTHOR
       Written and maintained by Paul Cuzner <pcuzner@ibm.com>.

REPORTING BUGS
       Patches and issues may be submitted to the IBM github repo at <https://github.ibm.com/ceph/atollon-utils>.'}]}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': 'c1e69f9dcb4f'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "[root@at11n1 ~]# atollon --help

summary: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'IBM Cloud has observed a significant limitation in the parallel throughput processing capabilities of ganesha with the Ceph FSAL. description: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'IBM Cloud has observed a significant limitation in the parallel throughput processing capabilities of ganesha with the Ceph FSAL. It appears that no more than 64 client I/O threads can be processed concurrently across all exports. This means that if a single ganesha instance is serving 16 exports, contention is seen when clients are sending I/O on any more than 4 threads each. This behavior can even be observed for a single export and single client running > 64 concurrent I/O threads, but the general concern from an IBM Cloud perspective is when we have many exports being served by the same ganesha instance. Initial investigation has seemingly determined that the bottleneck is in the libcephfs client connection in the Ceph FSAL and this limit isn’t being caused by the ganesha front end.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'f7c1fff5e746'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'This has been observed on downstream IBM Storage Ceph 8.1 and 9.0.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '4fdd0af75d91'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Many details on this problem and current investigation are in this Slack channel: '}, {'type': 'inlineCard', 'attrs': {'url': 'https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C09U32QLJNA', 'localId': 'd77049314397'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' '}], 'attrs': {'localId': '1028c51adcb4'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Please contact Scott Brewer / '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'brewers@us.ibm.com', 'marks': [{'type': 'link', 'attrs': {'href': 'mailto:brewers@us.ibm.com'}}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' / @brewers if you require access'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '05095ef28632'}}]}

Running “fs clone status” command then would then print “Error ENOENT: subvolume ‘<clone-subvol-name>' does not exist”."}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' Along with deleting the clone subvolume, its auth metadata file would also need to be deleted. Running “fs subvolume rm <some-subvol-name>” deletes the auth metadata file along with the subvolume normally. The auth metadata file lives in “/volumes” directory. If subvolume name is, say, “sv1”, its path would be “/volumes/_:sv1.meta”. Please take care of this detail too.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Having been through logs it’s not apparent how did the subvolume end up in this situation. comments.author: Aarti Sharma
comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'mention', 'attrs': {'id': '712020:5965a266-4d19-492f-834f-a8c0067cee64', 'text': '@Paul Cuzner', 'accessLevel': '', 'localId': 'ec2b59ff-fa52-4b89-b6c6-e93b21696590'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '  I agree that hardcoding RPM thresholds would create a maintenance issue if FRU or BMC updates modify the fan limits.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '6597dd73d14e'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'However, from customer perspective, the concern here is less about the raw RPM value itself and more about understanding whether a fan is operating normally or trending toward a critical condition. even displaying the current RPM alongside the configured critical thresholds, or highlighting fans that are approaching the critical limit, would give customers additional context beyond a raw RPM number and help them take proactive action before a fan failure is reported in the Cooling State panel.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Rather using static thresholds, could we consider deriving the status dynamically from the low/high critical values already exposed by the BMC/FRU (if available)? or check with the hardware team from where we can derive the critical values?'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '9c8efb2c6aa2'}}]}

comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Hi Pawan,'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Yes, we are aware of this problem: PG merging makes the PGs unavailable for a long period. The autoscaler here is doing what it is supposed to, however, there are certain scenarios (such as this one) where the bulk flag causes more inconvenience than convenience.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': "We can try to find a solution to alleviate this issue. But for now, I believe the workaround can set the autoscaler mode to `warn` when creating the pools such that it won't automatically scale the PGs. Once all pools are successfully created we can turn the autoscaler back on such that we catch only the scaling part of the autoscaling. If this in theory works then this should solve the PG availability issue."}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Thanks, Neha for moving it out to 8.1.'}]}]}

summary: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Investigate why Onode lookup accounts for a large portion of SeaStore’s transaction build phase, based on the newly added transaction phase metrics. The Onode Tree maps ghobject_t to the object’s Onode, and this lookup is a required part of building many user transactions, so reducing its cost could have meaningful impact on write-path latency.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'db61dc779343'}},...
description: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Investigate why Onode lookup accounts for a large portion of SeaStore’s transaction build phase, based on the newly added transaction phase metrics. The Onode Tree maps ghobject_t to the object’s Onode, and this lookup is a required part of building many user transactions, so reducing its cost could have meaningful impact on write-path latency.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'db61dc779343'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'attrs': {'localId': '892c0aa24bc2'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The work should start with measurement: break down the Onode lookup cost, identify whether the overhead comes from cache misses, B-tree traversal, decoding, transaction integration, or repeated lookups for the same object. Based on the findings, possible solutions should be evaluated before implementation.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'a2ac8512909a'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Two initial directions to investigate are:'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'defdcbe67254'}}, {'type': 'bulletList', 'content': [{'type': 'listItem', 'attrs': {'localId': 'ccf7f2f6a752'}, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'caching Onodes in the OBC to avoid repeated Onode Tree lookups when the object context is already available;'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '4820702099cc'}}]}, {'type': 'listItem', 'attrs': {'localId': '8b2c8aab9e67'}, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'improving the B-tree lookup implementation itself if traversal or lookup mechanics are the main source of overhead.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'c0239ce1b74d'}}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': '13d07a49f317'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'A key part of the task is to validate that any proposed optimization is better than the current implementation, both in complexity and performance. Implementation should proceed only after measurements clearly show the bottleneck and the selected approach provides a justified benefit.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '6403e491302f'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Expected outcome:', 'marks': [{'type': 'strong'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' A measured explanation for the high Onode lookup cost during transaction build, followed by a validated optimization proposal and implementation if the benefit is clear.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '52d95d195640'}}]}

comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Internal '}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'mention', 'attrs': {'id': '712020:0602f1f0-07ff-43ab-b637-833f1b99dd32', 'text': '@Prashant Dhange', 'accessLevel': '', 'localId': '0f3af305-2553-4213-b76e-3e8e318788a2'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ', kindly review the findings and share your insights.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Analysed the dashboard “No Data” issue observed after upgrading from RHCS 5.3 to 7.1z1.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'The root cause is that ceph-exporter was introduced starting in 6.1,( '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'What is ceph-exporter daemon in RHCS 6 cluster? - Red Hat Customer Portal', 'marks': [{'type': 'link', 'attrs': {'href': 'https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7129278'}}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ') so clusters on 5.3 never had this service. During upgrade, cephadm preserves the existing service layout and does not automatically deploy newly introduced optional services. As a result, ceph-exporter is not deployed post-upgrade, Prometheus cannot collect performance metrics, and dashboard graphs appear empty.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Workaround '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '[Ceph] ceph-exporter is not getting deployed during upgrades', 'marks': [{'type': 'link', 'attrs': {'href': 'https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7059378'}}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' - Red Hat Customer Portal as per this (manually deploy service ) resolves the issue immediately.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': "ceph orch apply ceph-exporter --placement='*'"}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'This is expected behavior and not a functional defect. However, if we still have a considerable number of customers upgrading from versions below 6.1, this situation is likely to repeat and result in recurring support cases.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'See two possible options to address this gap:', 'marks': [{'type': 'strong'}]}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Option 1', 'marks': [{'type': 'strong'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' – Documentation Update (Immediate & Low Risk)'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Open a documentation bug to update the upgrade guides (5.x → 6.x / 7.x ) and explicitly add a post-upgrade step to deploy ceph-exporter, for example:'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '“'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': "ceph orch apply ceph-exporter --placement='*'", 'marks': [{'type': 'em'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '”'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'This would ensure customers upgrading from versions below 6.1 are aware of the required step and can avoid the “Dashboard shows No Data” issue.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Option 2', 'marks': [{'type': 'strong'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' – Enhancement (Better Upgrade Experience)'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'If we have a significant number of customers still on versions < 6.1, we could consider opening an RFE for cephadm to:'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Detect upgrades from pre-6.1 releases'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Automatically deploy ceph-exporter when the monitoring stack is enabled'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'This would:'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Prevent repeated support escalations,Maintain backward compatibility\xa0'}]}]}

comments.author: Kushal Deb
comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Hi All,'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '9195bb62224c'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'I explored the replicated CRUSH rule behavior based on '}, {'type': 'mention', 'attrs': {'id': '70121:0aac4bfd-40e5-40f5-a497-2dbbe8d09978', 'text': '@Bill Scales', 'accessLevel': '', 'localId': '0a2259b0-2956-4e5e-a2ef-e1c4f7cd6ac2'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': "'s suggestion and the points discussed around service-created pools. I’m sharing my current understanding and the test observations here to confirm whether this aligns with the expected direction for this JIRA."}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'eb0feda0e44f'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'There are two related pieces of work:', 'marks': [{'type': 'underline'}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': '8d0d7929ecdd'}}, {'type': 'orderedList', 'attrs': {'order': 1, 'localId': 'e25f6e07bd0d'}, 'content': [{'type': 'listItem', 'attrs': {'localId': 'e9dee855ac82'}, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'inlineCard', 'attrs': {'url': 'https://ibm-ceph.atlassian.net/browse/ISCE-5077', 'localId': '239eb7e5588a'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' '}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'This is the foundation. Provisioner detects FCM devices from inventory and generates the OSD spec with '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'crush_device_class: fcm', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ', so that OSDs are created under the correct CRUSH device class. This part is already merged.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'cd737625b400'}}]}, {'type': 'listItem', 'attrs': {'localId': '924cf983eefd'}, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'IBMCEPH-14899', 'marks': [{'type': 'link', 'attrs': {'href': 'https://ibm-ceph.atlassian.net/browse/IBMCEPH-14899'}}, {'type': 'strong'}]}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'This appears to build on top of 5077. Once FCM devices are detected, Provisioner could create an FCM-specific replicated CRUSH rule and set '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'osd_pool_default_crush_rule', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' to that rule. It could also update the default EC profile to use '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'crush-device-class=fcm', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '04385003bbc2'}}]}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'To validate the replicated rule part, I tried this on a test cluster by emulating an FCM device class. After creating an FCM-specific replicated CRUSH rule and setting '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'osd_pool_default_crush_rule', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' to that rule, newly created replicated pools automatically picked up the FCM rule.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '3b9fb5a43c0a'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'I also deployed RGW after changing the default rule. The RGW-created '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '.rgw.root', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' pool picked up the FCM rule as well. So, from this test, service-created replicated pools can inherit the updated default rule, as long as the default is changed before those pools are created.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '56ad0207462c'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'One limitation is that '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'osd_pool_default_crush_rule', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' is still a single global default. It can make future replicated pools use FCM by default, but it cannot make per-service or per-pool placement decisions.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'a18d849ace39'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'For example, in a mixed FCM + TLC/QLC setup, if the desired policy is something like:'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '37fbf50afd33'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': '6205960a-43c4-465d-8b53-5146917d5663'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'RGW metadata/index -> TLC\nRGW data           -> FCM/QLC'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'then one global default rule would not be enough. Any service-created replicated pool that relies on the default would use the same rule. So mixed-media placement would still need explicit per-pool rule assignment, pre-created pools with the correct rules, or additional service/provisioner logic.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '331de18d33ed'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Mapping this back to the scenarios, my understanding is:', 'marks': [{'type': 'underline'}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'ed900189acb5'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Scenario 1: TLC-only system', 'marks': [{'type': 'strong'}]}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'No FCM is detected, so Provisioner should not create FCM-specific OSD specs or change replicated/EC defaults. Existing behavior remains unchanged.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '2597c4be321f'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Scenario 2: FCM-only system', 'marks': [{'type': 'strong'}]}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'This looks like the common Atollon case. Provisioner can detect FCM, create the FCM OSD spec, create an FCM-specific replicated rule, set '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'osd_pool_default_crush_rule', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' to that rule, and update the default EC profile to use FCM. title: CLONE - cephadm parallel deploy/remove can result in multiple identical ganeshas running at the same time causing EIO in client apps
summary: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Description of problem - Provide a detailed description of the issue encountered, including logs/command-output snippets and screenshots if the issue:'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'abb295098e73'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The design/architecture of ganesha HA-NFS is based on an assumption that multiple ganeshas with same identity are never running at the same...
description: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Description of problem - Provide a detailed description of the issue encountered, including logs/command-output snippets and screenshots if the issue:'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'abb295098e73'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The design/architecture of ganesha HA-NFS is based on an assumption that multiple ganeshas with same identity are never running at the same time.\xa0 We need the parallel deploy/remove code in cephadm to guarantee that when a ganesha is moved to another node, a ganesha instance with identity A, must be removed on the source node before ganesha with identity A can be started on the target node.  Running multiple ganeshas with the same identity causes multiple problems for HA-NFS failover scenarios:'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '34b5ad665b9d'}}, {'type': 'bulletList', 'content': [{'type': 'listItem', 'attrs': {'localId': 'e33e886bcc80'}, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The ganesha running on the source node has its MDS session hijacked by the ganesha starting on the target node.  This causes ganesha to return NFS4ERR_IO and NFS4ERR_SERVERFAULT protocol  errors to the client which result in the app seeing EIO.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '34b5ad665b9d'}}]}, {'type': 'listItem', 'attrs': {'localId': 'e33e886bcc80'}, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '“Dualing” identical ganeshas running on different nodes can result in mismanaged objects in RADOS for the grace table as well as persisted client records.  This can result in ganesha enforcing a full grace period when it should not because duplicate client records are persisted.   It can also result in EIO when ganesha is unable to open the client record object.'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'e3a2aeebefea'}}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': '2fb3d4e2f99a'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'In the short-term, we are working on an Acadia-specific workaround for the source-node ganesha EIO problem by removing networking from this ganesha before ever starting/deploying the target-node ganesha, but this is only solves part of the problem.   This workaround/hack is no help for problems related to multiple ganeshas inconsistently accessing/updating its RADOS objects.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'dc196b8f7033'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Version-Release number of selected component (if applicable):'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'dc196b8f7033'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'IBM cloud 8.x and 9.x releases'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '65c2fe04b570'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Does this issue impact your ability to continue to work with the product?'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '91abea6fa532'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Is there any workaround available to the best of your knowledge?'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '3122661ad1dd'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'See short-term partial workaround described above.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '3df8c77733a4'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Can this issue be reproduced? comments.body:
{'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'After reviewing the Ganesha logs again (including the latest debug logs), I am inclined towards a RADOS cluster grace period coordination deadlock causing NFS operations to hang indefinitely. The root cause seems to be a non-zero recovery epoch (rec) in the RADOS grace database preventing grace from lifting which blocks all file operations (OP_OPEN) with NFS4ERR_GRACE errors.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '3ebe34d1b413'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '[1] Initial Log Analysis of ganesha_nfs.log (Jun 12, 10:30:47)'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '07c5a8bb488e'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Log Location: /ecurep/sf/TS022/386/TS022386751/0-all_data/fileserver1_output_debug.log'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '0e90f2dae2ad'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The grace period starts at 10:30:47 with a 90-second configured duration. Export 1 creation fails with EPERM from ceph_start_reclaim() in src/FSAL/FSAL_CEPH/main.c:456, resulting in fsal_export being NULL and the export completely failing to initialize. Export 2 gets ENOENT which is expected for first-time setup and acceptable. The reaper thread continuously calls nfs_try_lift_grace() in src/SAL/nfs4_recovery.c every ~10 seconds with the pattern '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'check grace:reclaim complete(0) clid count(0)', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' indicating no clients and no active reclaims. Continuous HAProxy header failures are also observed indicating connection issues. Initial assessment shows Export 1 failed due to EPERM, but the grace period never lifts affecting ALL exports.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '3b974c845193'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': 'fd0834477cff'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '...
Jun 12 10:30:47 alwp0012 ganesha.nfsd-2[main] reclaim_reset :FSAL :EVENT :start_reclaim failed: (-1) Operation not permitted
Jun 12 10:30:47 alwp0012 ganesha.nfsd-2[main] load_export_config :CONFIG :CRIT :Could not create FSAL export for /volumes/_nogroup/nfs/9956bc34-578b-4abb-ae54-887214863183
Jun 12 10:30:47 alwp0012 ganesha.nfsd-2[reaper] nfs_try_lift_grace :STATE :EVENT :check grace:reclaim complete(0) clid count(0)
Jun 12 10:30:57 alwp0012 ganesha.nfsd-2[reaper] nfs_try_lift_grace :STATE :EVENT :check grace:reclaim complete(0) clid count(0)
Jun 12 10:31:07 alwp0012 ganesha.nfsd-2[reaper] nfs_try_lift_grace :STATE :EVENT :check grace:reclaim complete(0) clid count(0)

It's available in 9.0z3 but missing in 8.1z6"}], 'attrs': {'localId': '8aaaa847bdc3'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': 'f64795d3-6b28-4ec4-bb28-38ecf960631a'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '% git log -n1 147f7d569
commit 147f7d5695cb16041f245a8e3bbdf221b93035e8 (tag: nfs-ganesha-7.0-0.6.24)
Author: Sachin Punadikar <sachin.punadikar@ibm.com>
Date:   Mon Apr 27 13:47:33 2026 -0400

    Recovery: Handle zero clients condition in grace

    In a clustered grace setup, there are chances that a Ganesha having 0
    clients connected may come out of grace immediately and other Ganesha
    which has started grace will fail to detect that other Ganesha has
    enforced grace. Need to handle this situation and stop the Ganesha from
    quickly ending grace period.

    Resolves: IBMCEPH-14252

    Change-Id: I9f255edad99d322e819621f7ecd8a304fcd46968
    Signed-off-by: Sachin Punadikar <sachin.punadikar@ibm.com>'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'I may be wrong here but, this fix seems to directly addresses the exact scenario seen in the logs ('}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'clid_count = 0', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '). when there are no clients, ganesha keeps trying to lift grace immediately but if the RADOS backend is not ready ('}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'rec != 0', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '), those attempts keep failing, creating a loop where grace never exits.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '12939ab83068'}}]}

comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'We discussed a few options during the initial MCM days and the options that came were:'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '1. Mean'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': "a. Average doesn't depict outliers as state of cluster but also hides them."}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '2. Outlier in the cluster(to cover the case you are talking about)'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'a. This can be misleading if we consider a case where cluster has 100 nodes and 1 of them is running high on CPU. The entire cluster then will be represented as running high on CPU'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': '3. Xth percentile(90th ? )'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'a. This also will not necessarily be better than 2 depending on value of X'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'So, considering that, we have alerts for high CPU/memory utilizations at node level, we agreed it is better to show mean. Plus those alerts also manifest as clickable(for more details) counters on the UI.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Cc: @epuertat@redhat.com @gsitlani@redhat.com '}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'To bridge the 2 extremes, we could explore if we could cover max, min and mean. and on hover, we could show which nodes are on max CPU(if and only if thresholds are breached). '}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Please feel free to suggest here.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Cc: @ashwin.jadhav@ibm.com'}]}]}

comments.author: Ernesto Puerta Treceno
comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'The mean is extremely sensitive to big outliers (e.g.: 1 ms, 1 ms, 1 ms, 1 ms, 1000 ms = ~200 ms). In that case, neither the mean accurately describes the "average" situation (1ms vs. 200 ms) nor the worst case (200 ms if 5 times lesser than 1 second).'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'If we really want to have 2 orthogonal metrics to describe the usual/desired behaviour and also capture the "worst" cases I\'d go for: median/p50 and p99. In fact, we can define a configurable threshold under which the p99 is not shown (e.g.: less than 4x times the p50). That way, the user only sees the "average"/median unless there\'s some event (outlier) in which case they\'ll see the p99 metric as well. We can also describe/enhance this with colors (green p99 closer to p50, red if p99 > p50 x 4), charts, etc. Histograms work well too for percentiles but they bring more visual burden.'}]}]}

But visually how crowded the list would appear can be a matter of concern. I would let @ashwin.jadhav@ibm.com share the most relevant approach here.'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Copying from another discussion on another thread, @gsitlani@redhat.com says:'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "I had a chat with Gerald about this, we don't think we'll need per CPU detail. But one aggregate graph could for example: contain 3 metrics: min. CPU, avg. CPU and max. CPU. Same for RAM. That would still be a lot better than displaying e.g. 64 cores utilization individual. {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'mention', 'attrs': {'id': '712020:6db9cab6-71c5-4dff-bccd-f7bbeec30d14', 'text': '@Kritik Sachdeva', 'accessLevel': '', 'localId': 'd3285174-014a-4bee-b044-719e896f8b13'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' '}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'It will be difficult without the Flame graph to reach a conclusion. '}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'However, we can still try to find probable cause with the rest of the outputs requested. '}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Especially the perf counters from couple of OSDs that is having high CPU usage for 30 minutes. '}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Here is a sample script for collection : '}], 'attrs': {'localId': '21206d43114d'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': 'a3c5fc5a078f'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '#!/bin/bash

HOSTNAME=$(hostname -s)
LOG_DIR="/tmp/${HOSTNAME}.osd_ops_dump_data.$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S)"
SLEEP_TIME=60
RUN_TIME=500
osd_list="0 1 2"

mkdir -p $LOG_DIR
cd $LOG_DIR

CRUN=0
echo "Collecting ops dump data from all OSDs"
while [[ $CRUN -lt $RUN_TIME ]]
do
        CRUN=$(($CRUN + 1))
        for osd in ${osd_list}
        do
                ceph tell osd.$osd dump_historic_slow_ops > $LOG_DIR/osd.$osd-dump_historic_slow_ops.$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S).txt
                ceph tell osd.$osd dump_ops_in_flight > $LOG_DIR/osd.$osd-dump_ops_in_flight.$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S).txt
                ceph tell osd.$osd dump_historic_ops > $LOG_DIR/osd.$osd-dump_historic_ops.$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S).txt
                ceph tell osd.$osd perf dump > $LOG_DIR/osd.$osd-perf_dump.$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S).txt
                ceph tell osd.$osd dump_objectstore_kv_stats > $LOG_DIR/osd.$osd-dump_objectstore_kv_stats.$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S).txt
        done
        echo "Sleeping for $SLEEP_TIME seconds"
        sleep $SLEEP_TIME
done
echo "Kindly compress $LOG_DIR directory and attach it to the support case"'}]}]}

comments.body: {'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'mention', 'attrs': {'id': '712020:660723b6-1493-4917-b6cb-65556039df0a', 'text': '@Soumi Mitra', 'accessLevel': '', 'localId': 'dfbacd0f-69f0-48aa-aaf0-71c94186db81'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' this isn’t a ceph-volume bug.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '1bd32d982e82'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'OSDs 10 and 24 show osdspec_affinity “all-available-devices” because they were created under that spec, not because ceph-volume misassigned the affinity. The value is set at deployment time by cephadm and written at mkfs, ceph-volume only passes it through.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'b96fa0534bb3'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "The age gap in ‘ceph orch ls' (2 OSDs ~5 days old under ‘all-available-devices’ vs 46 OSDs ~11 weeks old under ‘uaeplus’) points to a recent creation of these two OSDs under the 'catch all spec’, not a cluster wide selection bug."}], 'attrs': {'localId': '254fc6f3ddf8'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': ' i see a couple of possible reasons :'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'b96fa0534bb3'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '1/ ‘osd.all-available-devices’ was still managed when these osds were created'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '29ffa2017b54'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '2/ automatic recreation after disk replacement or zap: if disks became available again while the spec ‘all-available-devices’ was managed, cephadm would automatically create new osds under that spec. (which is the documented declarative behavior of ‘ceph orch apply osd --all-available-devices’)'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '8db87b5ccc54'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "3/ the affected disks do not match the osd.uaeplus filters: uaeplus spec requires ‘data_devices: rotational: 1’ and ‘db_devices: rotational: 0’. If the disks behind OSDs 10 and 24 do not meet those criteria (device type and/or no available SSD for DB), only ‘all-available-devices’ (data_devices: all: true, host_pattern: '*') would accept them"}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'e55cc24bc249'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'attrs': {'localId': '4852b800e00a'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'By the way, cephadm documentation [1] explicitly warns against running “--all-available-devices” alongside custom OSD specs:'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '8b0efab02b9b'}}, {'type': 'blockquote', 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '"We recommend that advanced OSD specs include the service_id field. OSDs created using ceph orch daemon add or ceph orch apply osd --all-available-devices are placed in the plain osd service. Failing to include a service_id in your OSD spec causes the Ceph cluster to mix the OSDs from your spec with those OSDs, which can potentially result in the overwriting of service specs created by cephadm to track them."'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '55bf93388d46'}}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'ee06cf98787f'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Also, on the declarative behavior of ‘all-available-devices’ [2]:'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'bd0930ef889c'}}, {'type': 'blockquote', 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '"When you add new drives to the cluster, they will automatically be used to create new OSDs. When you remove an OSD and clean the LVM physical volume, a new OSD will be created automatically."'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'b0e224942f51'}}], 'attrs': {'localId': '8522ca166079'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'attrs': {'localId': '66972afc4baa'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': "This is expected behavior given two coexisting osd specs “all-available-devices” (host_pattern: '*', all: true) and “uaeplus” (restrictive filters).."}], 'attrs': {'localId': '72cc515ece2d'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'attrs': {'localId': '6b29c57ea104'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '[1] '}, {'type': 'inlineCard', 'attrs': {'url': 'https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/cephadm/services/osd/#advanced-osd-service-specifications', 'localId': '0b02aff3e3d0'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' '}], 'attrs': {'localId': '031c49fcbade'}}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '[2] '}, {'type': 'inlineCard', 'attrs': {'url': 'https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/cephadm/services/osd/#declarative-state', 'localId': '508f8a59523c'}}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' '}], 'attrs': {'localId': '792ee9ee4589'}}]}

Only other thing I’ll add is there is a command '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'ceph orch osd set-spec-affinity', 'marks': [{'type': 'code'}]}, {'type': 'text', 'text': ' that was added that marks OSDs as being tied to a different spec, although it isn’t present in all 7 releases, just the more recent ones. Beyond grouping them for service level commands what specs that OSDs have an affinity for is cosmetic.'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '2fbaddf0af1b'}}]}

{'type': 'doc', 'version': 1, 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Below commits have pushed'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '49319ff1ae6d'}}, {'type': 'blockquote', 'content': [{'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'commit 80f0053b2a9b2fe014c225c558c4c08665a4b895 (HEAD -> ceph-7.1-rhel-patches, origin/ceph-7.1-rhel-patches)'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Author: Goutham Pacha Ravi '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'gouthampravi@gmail.com', 'marks': [{'type': 'link', 'attrs': {'href': 'mailto:gouthampravi@gmail.com'}}]}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Date:   Mon May 18 10:58:27 2026 -0700'}], 'attrs': {'localId': '2ac643ccb37b'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': 'e5eb33f0ef51'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Allow /0 CIDR prefix in export client blocks

The lexer regex patterns for CIDR suffixes reject prefix
length 0 because they require the first digit to be [1-9].
This prevents valid CIDR notation like 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0
(RFC 4632, RFC 4291) from being used in export client
blocks to match all addresses in an address family.

Fix the regex to accept /0 while still disallowing leading
zeros.

Resolves: IBMCEPH-15730

Change-Id: Ibd5364266e7a5afe1b2749f9a5fc2c1dc7478ba3
Fixes: <https://github.com/nfs-ganesha/nfs-ganesha/issues/1396>
Signed-off-by: Goutham Pacha Ravi <gouthampravi@gmail.com>'}]}, {'type': 'paragraph', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'commit 3d210244bae3a46d2da303db765f9f7a92f4e755'}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Author: Peter Schwenke '}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'pschwenke@ddn.com', 'marks': [{'type': 'link', 'attrs': {'href': 'mailto:pschwenke@ddn.com'}}]}, {'type': 'hardBreak'}, {'type': 'text', 'text': 'Date:   Mon Aug 4 22:12:53 2025 +1000'}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'bd9a5672a5a3'}}, {'type': 'codeBlock', 'attrs': {'localId': '3c3f3b086419'}, 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Config Parsing: Allow 3 digit mask for IPv6 Export CIDRs

Allow CIDRs such as ::ffff:192.168.10.0/120 (
which is equivalent to 192.168.10.0/24) and
fe80::5a4d:7416:a595:bd6f/120.

CIDRs such as that will currently fail parsing.

Change-Id: I42d8be0d5b7143b8e53e63fbdddf0cd696bdd4c8
Signed-off-by: Peter Schwenke <pschwenke@ddn.com>'}]}], 'attrs': {'localId': 'e4ab5b1550a1'}}]}
